titre: New Jersey: In 1807, a Statute Reads Into the Constitution What It Does Not Say
accroche: In 1776, New Jersey gives the vote to all “inhabitants” with property. In 1807, a statute reserves it to white men, in the name of the constitution.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 16, 1807, the New Jersey legislature adopts a supplement to its 1797 election law. Its operative provision reserves the vote to free, white, male citizens aged twenty-one. The preamble, for its part, claims to change nothing: it wants only to say what the state constitution has always meant.

## A Word With No Sex and No Color

On July 2, 1776, the New Jersey Provincial Congress adopts a constitution without submitting it to the people. Its Article IV gives the right to vote for representatives to all “inhabitants” of the colony, of legal age, who own a net estate of at least fifty pounds and have lived in their county for twelve months. The text mentions neither sex, nor color, nor citizenship.

According to the National Park Service, women voted in the state in the 1790s and the early 1800s, but only unmarried women: according to the same source, a married woman could not own property in her own right. Black Americans could vote too, if they met the residency and wealth requirements. In 1797, the state requires voters to be free inhabitants.

## A Statute That Calls Itself Declaratory

The preamble of the 1807 statute invokes doubts and “great diversities in practice” in the state over whether to admit aliens, women, and people of color to the vote. It judges it “highly necessary to the safety, quiet, good order and dignity of the state” to remove these doubts by an act “declaratory of the true sense and meaning of the constitution,” in line with “the intent of the framers thereof.” Then the first section sets the condition: being a “free, white, male citizen.”

According to the National Park Service, the measure was meant to give an advantage to the Democratic-Republican Party in the presidential election of 1808, since women often voted for the opposing camp, the Federalists. It takes the state's new constitution of 1844 for the exclusion of women and Black Americans to be written into the constitution itself.

## What This Changes

We like to tell the story of women's suffrage as a conquest that advances in steps. New Jersey shows the opposite path: a right that the text does not deny, exercised for years, then withdrawn by an ordinary statute.

The method matters as much as the result. By presenting itself as an interpretation, the 1807 statute does not officially revise Article IV: it claims to read it correctly. The legislature makes itself the judge of the meaning of a constitution that constrains it, and it changes the rule without presenting itself as a reviser. That “inhabitants” meant men only in 1776 is an assertion of the 1807 statute, not a fact established by the 1776 text.

Can an assembly correct its reading of a constitution without revising it, and who, then, protects the text against it?

repere.texte: The New Jersey constitution of July 2, 1776 grants the vote to the colony's “inhabitants,” of legal age, who meet a wealth and residency requirement. The statute of November 16, 1807 declares itself “declaratory of the true sense and meaning of the constitution” and reserves it to “free, white, male citizen[s].”
repere.source: Laws of the State of New Jersey, Trenton, 1811, p. 33: statute of November 16, 1807 (excerpt published by the University of Nebraska–Lincoln)

carte.punch: 1776: the vote to “inhabitants,” with no sex or color. 1807: a statute says no.
carte.idee: The 1776 New Jersey constitution mentions neither sex nor color: unmarried women voted under it. On November 16, 1807, a statute reserves the vote to free white men, presenting itself as the faithful interpretation of that text, without revising it.

quiz.question: How does the 1807 New Jersey statute justify excluding women from voting?
choix: It formally revises Article IV of the 1776 constitution
It applies a ruling of the state supreme court on the meaning of the word “inhabitants”
It presents itself as a declaration of the true meaning of the constitution, without amending it
It relies on the 1787 federal Constitution, which reserves the vote to men
quiz.explication: The preamble invokes doubts and an act “declaratory of the true sense” of the constitution: the statute claims to read Article IV, not to revise it. It cites no court decision, and the 1787 federal Constitution does not set who votes in the states. It takes until 1844 for the state constitution to write the exclusion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did one have to meet in order to vote under the 1776 New Jersey constitution?
choix: Be an “inhabitant” of legal age, with fifty pounds of net estate and twelve months of residence
Be a free white man who owned farmland in the state
Be a United States citizen for at least five years and know how to read
Belong to one of the founding families recognized by the Provincial Congress
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article IV granted the vote to every “inhabitant” of legal age who owned at least fifty pounds of net estate and had lived in their county for twelve months, with no mention of sex or color.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the National Park Service, who was able to vote in New Jersey in the 1790s and the early 1800s, besides men?
choix: Married women, who owned land in their husbands' names
Unmarried women and Black Americans who met the residency and wealth requirements
Recently arrived foreigners, with no residency requirement
Minors over sixteen, sponsored by a county landowner
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the National Park Service, unmarried women and Black Americans voted in the state in this period, provided they met the residency and wealth criteria; a married woman could not own property in her own right.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the National Park Service, what political goal did the 1807 statute pursue?
choix: To prepare the abolition of slavery in the state ahead of the rest of the Union
To end electoral fraud found in the 1800 election
To favor the Democratic-Republican Party in 1808, since women often voted Federalist
To align New Jersey with the 1787 federal Constitution on suffrage
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the National Park Service, the 1807 statute was meant to give an advantage to the Democratic-Republican Party in the presidential election of 1808, since women often voted for the opposing camp, the Federalists.
